source.title: CoSy: Evaluating Textual Explanations of Neurons
source.authors: Laura Kopf; P. Bommer; Anna Hedström; Sebastian Lapuschkin; M. Höhne; Kirill Bykov

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether textual descriptions of neurons align with neuron responses, and finds substantial variation: some methods score near random while others score highly. This refines the broad claim that textual neuron explanations reliably describe neuron behavior, but it uses computer-vision models and synthetic images rather than language-model neurons and text.
record.gate_note: Table 3 reports explanation-quality scores for three methods across six model/dataset settings; these are recorded separately by model, method, and metric. The paper also reports output-neuron true-versus-random sanity checks, but those test the scoring framework on known class labels rather than the explanation-failure claim. Layer-sweep results in Figure 4 are described as trends in the text but individual plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: V6 is tested in a new setting, vision models rather than language models. MILAN and FALCON build their explanations from a neuron's highly activating images or regions. When CoSy turns those explanations into synthetic images, they fail to make the neuron fire: AUC is close to 0.5 (random). CLIP-Dissect also uses top-activating images, yet its explanations do predict firing. The authors also argue directly that top-activating examples reflect only the maximum tail of a neuron's activations.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that CoSy reliably separates true explanations from random ones. Explanation quality varies sharply by method: INVERT and CLIP-Dissect score high, while MILAN and FALCON are near random and can mislead. Neuron description methods work best in the last layers and worse in lower layers.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates computer-vision neuron descriptions by generating synthetic images from their text and comparing model activations with control-image activations using AUC and MAD. It does not audit language-model neurons or evaluate explanations on new text.
record.method_sensitivity: Explanation scores vary by method and model/dataset. The text reports generally higher scores for later ResNet18 layers than lower layers, and describes prompt choice and text-to-image model as affecting generated-image similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: In ResNet18, explanation quality falls in lower layers for all four methods; later layers score highest.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Textual neuron explanations predict firing less well in early vision layers than in late ones.

record.problems: The evidence is from computer-vision models and generated images, not language-model neurons or new text. The study evaluates 50 randomly selected neurons per setting. The paper notes limitations of text-to-image generation, particularly for abstract concepts, and that its evaluation measures do not exhaust explanation quality.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 36 Table 3 metric results. Figure 4's layer-by-layer scores are not separately recorded because the supplied text gives only a qualitative description of the plotted results, not individual values.

untested.parts: Language-model neurons, and firing on new text; only vision models and synthetic images are tested.
Entire version: no Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit.
Entire version: no language-model scale or dense-versus-MoE comparison.
Entire version: no InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis.
Entire version: no estimate of interpretable-neuron shares by architecture, regularization or tool.
Entire version: no simulation-based scoring on text.

missing.what: Layer-by-layer AUC and MAD in ResNet18 for MILAN, FALCON, CLIP-Dissect and INVERT. FALCON, which also uses top-activating images, sits at about 0.5 AUC. The text gives no per-layer values.
FALCON scores on its original 'explainable neurons' subset (7, 5 and 15 neurons in layers 2–4).
The authors' argument that top-activating images reflect only the maximum tail, not the neuron's overall behaviour.

record.verdict_notes: This is a vision-only study, so its bearing on V6 is indirect. MILAN's low scores may partly reflect text-to-image failure on abstract labels such as 'white areas'. CoSy itself is the study's method, and INVERT is by overlapping authors. INVERT rows are unlinked because INVERT does not derive explanations from activating examples. The output-neuron sanity checks in Table 2 are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or estimate of one-job, two-job, or not-understood neuron poles.
No language-model scaling comparison, dense-versus-MoE comparison, or trillion-parameter models.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose interpretation, or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No comparison of architecture or regularization as causes of neuron interpretability, nor estimates of interpretable-neuron shares for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
No attribution graphs or test of whether a large model's own neurons suffice as circuit units.
Tests textual neuron descriptions against responses to generated images in vision models, not explanations explicitly fitted to activating examples in language models or their firing on new text.
Scoring is done on synthesized images, not by simulating neuron activations on new text; the paper does not test the stated language-model claim or its minority-good-score characterization.

relationships.condition: MILAN explanations, built from top-activating image regions, in the second-to-last layer of six vision models
relationships.reason: MILAN AUC is 0.44–0.61 in most settings and MAD is near zero, so explanations fit to activating regions do not predict firing (T3-R01, R02, R07, R08, R13, R14, R19, R20, R25, R26). The paper partly blames text-to-image limits on abstract concepts.
relationships.display_finding: MILAN AUC was 0.44–0.61 in most settings with MAD near zero, so explanations fitted to activating regions did not predict firing. The paper partly blames limits of text-to-image generation on abstract concepts.

source_check.reason: MILAN AUC 0.44-0.61 and MAD -0.08 to 0.69 in five of six models (rows R01-R26). Paper: average AUC below 0.65, close to random guessing, poor in all settings. The condition says six models, but Places365 ResNet50 (R31/R32) is under l1.

relationships.condition: CLIP-Dissect explanations, which also use the most highly activated images, in the same layers
relationships.reason: CLIP-Dissect AUC is 0.78–0.95 and MAD 1.29–4.98 (T3-R03, R04, R09, R10, R15, R16, R21, R22, R27, R28, R33, R34), so the failure depends on the explanation method. MILAN's 0.65 on Places365 ResNet50 is also only a partial failure (T3-R31, R32).
relationships.display_finding: CLIP-Dissect reached AUC 0.78–0.95 and MAD 1.29–4.98, so the failure depends on the explanation method. MILAN scored 0.65 on Places365 ResNet50, which is also only a partial failure.

relation.reason: Its own CoSy results on MILAN and CLIP-Dissect bear on whether explanations built from top-activating images predict firing.

tranche.reason: New setting (vision CNNs/ViTs) with its own results bearing on V6. The paper does not argue against any version, so T5 does not fit.

source_check.notes: Authors partly blame MILAN's low scores on text-to-image limits for abstract explanations ('white areas', 'nothing'). CoSy never checks that MILAN's descriptions fit the top-activating images. INVERT optimizes AUC, which may bias its scores.
